content: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections and, in some cases, to prevent certain bacterial infections. It is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold or flu. This medication is typically administered intravenously, as directed by a healthcare provider, usually every six hours. The injection should be given slowly over 20 to 60 minutes. It is intended for short-term use until the patient can transition to oral antibiotics or complete their treatment. Patients using erythromycin at home should be thoroughly instructed by their healthcare provider on preparation and administration. The solution should be visually inspected for particles or discoloration before use, and any compromised product should be discarded. For optimal effectiveness, erythromycin should be administered at evenly spaced intervals. If prescribed for an infection, the full course of treatment must be completed, even if symptoms improve after a few days, to prevent the recurrence of the infection. If used for prevention, it must be taken exactly as directed by the physician. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, and redness or pain at the injection site. While these are generally mild, erythromycin may rarely cause severe intestinal conditions due to Clostridium difficile (C. diff) bacteria, which can occur during or even weeks to months after treatment. Prolonged or repeated use may lead to oral thrush or vaginal yeast infections. Serious allergic reactions are rare but possible. Erythromycin may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine, and can cause a condition affecting heart rhythm known as QT prolongation. This risk is higher in individuals with certain medical conditions, low potassium or magnesium levels, or those taking medications that also prolong the QT interval. Babies may be at increased risk for a serious stomach condition called infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS). Parents should contact their physician if vomiting or irritability with feeding occurs. During pregnancy, erythromycin should only be used when clearly necessary, as it passes into breast milk. Caution is advised when prescribing this medication to patients with impaired liver function, as it is primarily excreted by the liver. Erythromycin therapy has been associated with exacerbation of symptoms in patients with myasthenia gravis and may cause new-onset symptoms of myasthenic syndrome. Drug interactions are a significant consideration with erythromycin. It can increase the levels or effects of other medications by slowing their removal from the body. Examples include drugs metabolized by the CYP3A4 enzyme, such as certain statins (lovastatin, simvastatin), ergotamine, and dihydroergotamine. Co-administration with these drugs should be avoided or closely monitored. Erythromycin may also interfere with certain laboratory tests, potentially causing false results. Patients should maintain a list of all medications and supplements they are taking and share it with their healthcare provider to avoid potential interactions. If an overdose occurs, immediate medical attention is required. In the U.S., contact 911 or a poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. Proper storage of erythromycin is essential. It should be kept at controlled room temperature, and expired or unused medication should be discarded appropriately. Patients should not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into drains unless instructed to do so. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about erythromycin. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice. Patients should always consult their healthcare provider for complete information tailored to their specific health needs.
